clinicalPearls: Presents as migratory, annular or polycyclic erythematous plaques with superficial erosions, crusting and a collarette of scale, favouring the perioral area, perineum, groin and distal limbs
Individual lesions evolve over days with central clearing while new lesions appear at the periphery, giving a waxing and waning pattern
It is the classic cutaneous marker of the glucagonoma syndrome, a glucagon-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour
Associated features include weight loss, diabetes or glucose intolerance, glossitis, angular cheilitis, anaemia and venous thrombosis
Hypoaminoacidaemia is characteristic and may drive the skin changes, and similar rashes occur in other states of nutritional deficiency
Biopsy shows necrosis of the upper epidermis with pallor of the upper keratinocytes, vacuolisation and confluent parakeratosis
Treatment is resection of the glucagonoma where possible, with somatostatin analogues and amino-acid, zinc and fatty-acid repletion
reference.pathophysiology: Necrolytic migratory erythema is most often a paraneoplastic manifestation of a glucagon-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour. Sustained hyperglucagonaemia promotes catabolism with depletion of amino acids, and the resulting hypoaminoacidaemia, together with deficiencies of zinc and essential fatty acids, is thought to impair epidermal integrity. Nutrient-starved keratinocytes in the upper epidermis undergo necrolysis, producing the characteristic superficial necrosis, vacuolisation and crusting. Similar changes can arise in non-tumour states of malnutrition, malabsorption or liver disease that share these deficiencies.
additionalDifferentials: Pellagra and other nutritional deficiency dermatoses
additionalInvestigations: Pancreatic imaging (CT/MRI) and functional neuroendocrine imaging to localise the tumour
Plasma amino-acid profile, serum zinc and essential fatty acid status
Skin biopsy for the characteristic epidermal necrolysis
Full blood count for normochromic anaemia and general nutritional screen
redFlags: Weight loss, new diabetes and rash together, pointing to glucagonoma
Venous thromboembolism, which is common and potentially fatal in the glucagonoma syndrome
Evidence of metastatic neuroendocrine disease at diagnosis
Severe malnutrition with extensive skin breakdown and secondary infection
reference.prognosis: When a glucagonoma is localised and resected the rash and metabolic disturbances usually resolve, but many tumours have already metastasised at diagnosis, which worsens the outlook; nutritional and somatostatin-based measures can improve the skin and symptoms even when cure is not possible.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating the rash as eczema, psoriasis or candidiasis and missing the underlying tumour
Not measuring glucagon and amino acids in a suggestive migratory erosive eruption
Overlooking the high risk of venous thrombosis in affected patients
Attributing all cases to a tumour and ignoring nutritional or hepatic causes of a similar picture
management: Surgical resection of the glucagonoma, which is potentially curative and clears the rash when the tumour is localised
Somatostatin analogues such as octreotide or lanreotide to suppress glucagon secretion and improve the eruption
Correction of the underlying deficiencies with amino acid, zinc and essential fatty acid repletion
Management of diabetes or glucose intolerance and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis given the thrombotic risk
Systemic therapy for unresectable or metastatic disease, including peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, targeted agents or chemotherapy
Management through a neuroendocrine tumour multidisciplinary team with surveillance imaging
